findings.issue_text: [High/data] lib/validators/email_validator.rb:13 — `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a DB write from inside a validation; when called via `User#save`, a blocked email fails validation, `with_transaction_returning_status` raises `ActiveRecord::Rollback`, and the nested `record.save` is rolled back, so `match_count`/`last_match_at` are lost in exactly the block case. The spec only calls `should_block?` directly and doesn't catch this.

[Medium/security] lib/validators/email_validator.rb:20 — `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)` is unanchored and only escapes `.`, so a whitelist of `example.com` accepts `user@example.com.evil.org` and other regex metacharacters in the setting are interpreted; should anchor with `@(...)\z` and use `Regexp.escape`.

[Medium/bug] app/models/blocked_email.rb:12 — `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` is an exact, case-sensitive match with no normalization while the domain whitelist/blacklist is case-insensitive, so `Block@SpamFromHome.org` bypasses a block on `block@spamfromhome.org`; the unique index on `blocked_emails.email` likewise allows case-variant duplicates.

[Medium/bug] app/models/blocked_email.rb:11 — `should_block?` has side effects on every validation pass, and `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` fires on any `valid?`/`save` attempt (repeated failed submits, admin edits), so `match_count` is inflated by every validation run rather than every real signup attempt.

[Low/concurrency] app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — `match_count += 1; save` is a non-atomic read-modify-write; concurrent signups with the same blocked email lose increments. Use `increment!(:match_count)` or `update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, ...")`.
[Low/bug] app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — the return value of `record.save` is ignored; a failed save (e.g. a validation error on the BlockedEmail row) silently drops the stats update with no log.

[Low/api] app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — any server-side email error (uniqueness, blocked, domain not allowed) is surfaced as `user.email.invalid`, misstating the reason; the server's `errors.email` with the real message is discarded.

[Low/bug] app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:275 — the rejected-email check compares `result.values.email` (server-stored attribute) against `accountEmail` (raw client input) with `contains`; if the server strips or downcases the email, the values differ and the rejection never shows.

[Low/bug] app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` on the class definition puts a single array on the prototype shared by every controller instance; only safe while the controller is a singleton, should be initialized in `init`.

[Medium/test_gap] spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb — `should_block?` is stubbed, so there is no test that a `User` with a blocked email actually fails to save, no test that stats survive a failed `User#save`, no coverage of the whitelist/blacklist branches now in `EmailValidator`, and the new `errors`/`values` keys in `UsersController#create` are untested.

goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.

The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Medium/bug] app/models/blocked_email.rb:11 — `should_block?` has side effects on every validation pass, and `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` fires on any `valid?`/`save` attempt (repeated failed submits, admin edits), so `match_count` is inflated by every validation run rather than every real signup attempt.

adjudication.rationale: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` (app/models/blocked_email.rb) increments `match_count` and persists `last_match_at` every time it is called, and the new `EmailValidator` invokes it during validation (`validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` in app/models/user.rb). This makes the counter reflect “number of validation executions for a blocked email” rather than strictly “real signup attempts,” and it also introduces DB writes during validation. However, the diff doesn’t establish what `match_count` is intended to measure or that this causes functional breakage beyond potentially noisy statistics/extra writes, so it’s a grounded concern but not a clearly verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Low/concurrency] app/models/blocked_email.rb:14 — `match_count += 1; save` is a non-atomic read-modify-write; concurrent signups with the same blocked email lose increments. Use `increment!(:match_count)` or `update_all("match_count = match_count + 1, ...")`.

adjudication.rationale: In app/models/blocked_email.rb#should_block?, the code does `record.match_count += 1` followed by `record.save`. This is a classic non-atomic read-modify-write. If multiple signups hit the same blocked email concurrently, increments can be lost because each request reads the same old match_count and overwrites the other’s update. An atomic update (e.g., `increment!` or `update_all` with `match_count = match_count + 1`) would avoid the race.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Low/bug] app/models/blocked_email.rb:16 — the return value of `record.save` is ignored; a failed save (e.g. a validation error on the BlockedEmail row) silently drops the stats update with no log.

adjudication.rationale: In `BlockedEmail.should_block?`, when a matching record is found it increments `match_count`/sets `last_match_at` and calls `record.save`, but does not check the return value or handle failures (no log/exception handling). While validations/db constraints make a failure unlikely in normal cases, the diff does show the save result is ignored, so the robustness concern is grounded but not a clearly verifiable functional bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Low/api] app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:69 — any server-side email error (uniqueness, blocked, domain not allowed) is surfaced as `user.email.invalid`, misstating the reason; the server's `errors.email` with the real message is discarded.

adjudication.rationale: In create_account_controller.js, when the server returns any email-related error (checked only via `result.errors && result.errors.email`), the client pushes that email into `rejectedEmails` and subsequent validation always returns `failed: true` with `reason: I18n.t('user.email.invalid')`. The diff also adds server-side specific email errors/messages (`user.email.not_allowed`, `user.email.blocked`, uniqueness, etc.) via `errors: user.errors.to_hash`, but the client does not surface those per-field messages and instead uses the generic `user.email.invalid`, which can misstate the actual reason (e.g., blocked vs invalid format).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Low/bug] app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:275 — the rejected-email check compares `result.values.email` (server-stored attribute) against `accountEmail` (raw client input) with `contains`; if the server strips or downcases the email, the values differ and the rejection never shows.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add a client-side cache of rejected emails (`rejectedEmails`) and pushes `result.values.email` from the server into it, then checks `contains(accountEmail)`. However, nothing in the shown server-side changes indicates that the server strips or downcases the email before putting it into `user.attributes` (used for `values`). The new `EmailValidator` uses the raw `value` and does not normalize it. So the claimed mismatch due to server normalization is not verifiable from this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Low/bug] app/assets/javascripts/discourse/controllers/create_account_controller.js:17 — `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` on the class definition puts a single array on the prototype shared by every controller instance; only safe while the controller is a singleton, should be initialized in `init`.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` directly on the controller class definition (prototype). In Ember, that means the same array instance can be shared across multiple controller instances if more than one is ever created, since it’s not initialized per-instance (e.g., in `init`). The diff itself doesn’t prove multiple instances will exist (controllers are often singletons), so it’s not a verifiable functional bug from the diff alone, but it is a specific, diff-grounded design risk worth addressing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [Medium/test_gap] spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb — `should_block?` is stubbed, so there is no test that a `User` with a blocked email actually fails to save, no test that stats survive a failed `User#save`, no coverage of the whitelist/blacklist branches now in `EmailValidator`, and the new `errors`/`values` keys in `UsersController#create` are untested.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds nontrivial behavior that is only partially covered by tests. In `spec/components/validators/email_validator_spec.rb`, `BlockedEmail.should_block?` is stubbed, so it does not exercise the real `BlockedEmail.should_block?` logic or any integration path where a `User` save fails due to `validates :email, email: true` in `app/models/user.rb`. The new whitelist/blacklist branches were moved into `lib/validators/email_validator.rb`, but the spec does not cover those branches at all. Additionally, `UsersController#create` now includes `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice(...)`, and the JS relies on `result.errors.email`/`result.values.email` to populate `rejectedEmails`, yet there is no test shown for this new response shape.
